A Family Dossier · December 19–28, 2026

Where We Go Together

Nine days for Alameda, Kilifi, and Atlanta to actually enjoy the holidays together — not just occupy the same room, which we can already do any time we like. Five routes, weighed against a shellfish allergy, a nine-month-old, two mid-70s grandparents, and two kids who'd rather see something than lie on a beach.

Stephen, Holly & Robin
ALAMEDA, CA · 9 MONTHS OLD
Lindsay, Ani, Ayaan & Laila
KILIFI, KENYA · AGES 11 & 12
Mom & Dad
ATLANTA, GA · MID-70S

Two things decide this before anything else

1.Skiing, or not. If it's in, that's Tahoe — nothing else on this list has it.

2.If it's not skiing: whether LALA wants room to see Siddu and Francis' family as part of the same trip, not a separate one. Mexico, Costa Rica, Tahoe, and New Orleans are all close enough to the US that this can be a natural add-on before or after. Spain isn't — it would be its own dedicated trip.

At a glance

Belize is out — not enough to fill nine days against these five. Every flight time is a rough door-to-door estimate for the long-haul leg. Mombasa column assumes a ~1hr drive from Kilifi, then MBA's own direct connections (Dubai, Doha, Addis, or Frankfurt) rather than backtracking through Nairobi first.

Route 01

Mexico City + Oaxaca

Nobody knows who actually built Teotihuacán. It isn't Aztec — the Aztecs arrived centuries after the city had already been abandoned and burned, found it in ruins, and named it themselves, believing the gods had been born there. Mexico City's Templo Mayor was found entirely by accident in 1978, when utility workers hit a carved stone disc a few blocks from the Zócalo and the government shut down a city block to dig. Oaxaca's weaving villages still dye wool with cochineal — a scale insect crushed for red pigment — and indigo, the same materials and the same hand process as five centuries ago, not a revival for tourists but a craft that never stopped.

Route4 nights CDMX → 4 nights Oaxaca
Link1hr flight, CDMX–OAX
Altitude7,350 ft — plan a slow Day 1
Allergy riskLow

Where to stay

You asked whether short-term rentals could realistically fit all eight of us — yes, comfortably, in both cities. Roma Norte and Condesa alone list more than 150 full houses on Airbnb, including several purpose-built for group reunions. Oaxaca's Centro Histórico has multiple colonial courtyard casas built for exactly this size of group. A rental also solves the allergy question better than any hotel: a real kitchen means Mom's meals aren't dependent on a restaurant getting it right.

Mexico City · Roma Norte / Condesa

A rented group house

Dozens of 4–8BR architect-renovated houses with rooftop terraces are listed here, built for reunions like this one — e.g. Casa Mera, an 8BR Roma Norte mansion sleeping up to 16.

~$600–1,200/night for the whole group
Oaxaca · Centro Histórico

A colonial courtyard casa

4-bedroom, 8-person houses two or three blocks from Santo Domingo, with private courtyards and full kitchens, are a normal listing category here — not a stretch to find.

~$300–500/night for the house

Day by day

DayFocusDetails
1ArriveSettle into the rental, easy walk around Roma/Condesa, early dinner.
2Historic centerZócalo, Metropolitan Cathedral, Palacio Nacional for the Diego Rivera murals — the full sweep of Mexican history on one wall. Templo Mayor ruins are steps away.
3Anthropology & the parkMuseo Nacional de Antropología in the morning — the world's foremost collection of Mesoamerican artifacts, including the Aztec Sun Stone. Chapultepec Park and Castle in the afternoon, stroller-friendly.
4TeotihuacánPrivate van, early start. Climb the Pyramid of the Sun (240 steps — optional; the view from the Avenue of the Dead is nearly as good for anyone who'd rather not). Carrier, not stroller, for the baby.Split option: grandparents can stay lower and closer to the van.
5Fly to Oaxaca1-hour flight. Afternoon walk to the Zócalo and Santo Domingo, whose gilded interior is one of the great Baroque church interiors in the Americas.
DayFocusDetails
6Monte AlbánA 1,500-year-old Zapotec capital on a leveled mountaintop. The central plaza is flat and easy for all ages; the surrounding temple mounds are optional climbs.
7Teotitlán del ValleA Zapotec weaving village, plus a mezcal tasting en route — flat, easy walking, living craft rather than a museum piece. If dates land on Dec 23: Noche de Rábanos in the Zócalo that evening — go early, plan an early exit with the baby.
8Split dayHierve el Agua (petrified waterfalls, but 100+ stairs down and back) for whoever wants it. San Bartolo Coyotepec pottery village — flat, easy, famous for its black clay — for grandparents and the baby.
9Depart—

Mezcal, if you want it

In Situ Mezcalería (Guerrero 413, Centro) is the easiest good option — a huge selection organized by agave type and still method (clay pot vs. copper), so you can actually compare rather than just sample, walk-in, open until 8pm most nights. For something more curated, La Mezcaloteca runs a guided tasting of small-batch mezcals from named producers rather than a general bar menu — appointment-only and books out weeks ahead, worth reserving before you leave home if you want it.

Meals & the allergy

Oaxacan food is mole- and corn-based, not seafood-forward — genuinely the easiest cuisine in this whole comparison for a severe shellfish allergy. Los Danzantes and Casa Oaxaca are good sit-down picks. In Mexico City, skip seafood-focused kitchens like Contramar; taco stands and tlayuda spots are safe defaults, and market marisco (seafood) stalls are easy to simply walk past.

Route 02

Costa Rica: Monteverde + Manuel Antonio

Swapped out Arenal since you, your parents, and Lindsay already covered that ground in 2010. Monteverde is a different Costa Rica entirely — cloud forest at 4,600 feet instead of volcano lowlands, moss-draped trees, light filtered green. It also has an actual story behind it: in 1951, a small group of Quaker settlers from Alabama bought land here and set a third of it aside as forest reserve rather than clearing it — one of the first deliberate conservation acts in Central America, and the root of the whole country's ecotourism identity.

Route5 nights Monteverde → 3 nights Manuel Antonio
Link~4hr private van transfer
Vs. 2010 tripNo Arenal overlap
Allergy riskLow inland, moderate coast

Where to stay

LALA still prefers a rental to separate hotel rooms — workable in both spots here without adding real distance from the attractions.

Monteverde

A rental villa near Santa Elena

Multi-bedroom villas with full kitchens exist 10–15 minutes outside town — close enough to the reserves and the cheese factory that it doesn't cost real time. If nothing with enough bedrooms turns up for your dates, Hotel Belmar is the fallback: a 40-year family-run hotel just named #3 in Travel + Leisure's World's Best Awards for 2026, with 1,000+ sq ft Nicoya Suites.

Rental preferred · hotel as backup
Manuel Antonio

A rental villa

This one's easier — Manuel Antonio has a deep market of 4–5BR villas with private pools and ocean views (Casa Reserva, in the La Reserva community, is representative of the category), most a short drive from the park entrance.

Rental preferred · Arenas del Mar (5-star, beachfront) as backup

Day by day

DayFocusDetails
1–2Arrive & transferLand San José, transfer to Monteverde (~3h, scenic).
3Canopy & cheeseSelvatura or Sky Walk hanging bridges through the cloud forest canopy — paved in sections, stroller-manageable. Afternoon: the Monteverde Cheese Factory, started by the same Quaker settlers — try the cheese, hear the history.
4Coffee, then splitCafé Monteverde working-farm tour, easy walking, hands-on for the tweens.Split: adults + tweens zipline the canopy; grandparents and the baby visit the Hummingbird Gallery — feeders swarming a dozen species at arm's length.
5Curi-Cancha ReserveA quieter, easier-walking reserve than the main Monteverde entrance, with good odds of a resplendent quetzal sighting with a guide.
6Transfer to the coast~4hr private van to Manuel Antonio, stopping at the Tarcoles River bridge to see the crocodiles from above.
DayFocusDetails
7Manuel Antonio N.P.Guided boardwalk walk — sloths and white-faced monkeys nearly guaranteed. Timed-entry ticket required; book ahead for the holiday week.
8Beach dayPlaya Biesanz or the resort's own beach.Split option: a mangrove boat tour on Damas Island.
9Transfer & departBack to San José, depart.

Meals & the allergy

Inland in Monteverde, menus lean vegetable- and dairy-forward — thank the same cheesemaking history — and shellfish risk is genuinely low. On the Pacific coast at Manuel Antonio, ceviche is everywhere; call ahead and ask about shared fryers and stock at every restaurant, every visit.

Route 03

Alameda + Lake Tahoe

The easy button — and still a real first for Ayaan and Laila: they've seen snow before, but never clipped into a board or skis. Stephen's a solid intermediate snowboarder, so this doesn't need to be a week of ski school — he can take over leading runs himself once they've got the basics down. There's real San Francisco history folded in too, not just the mountain.

Route3–4 nights Alameda → 5 nights Tahoe
LinkDrive, build in a weather buffer day
On the slopesAyaan & Laila's first time skiing/riding
Allergy riskLow

Where to stay

Our place in Alameda isn't big enough to host all eight of us, so LALA and the grandparents will need their own rental for the Bay Area stretch. For the mountain stretch, South Lake Tahoe is the easy default — the Gondola and the sno-park below are both built around it. Donner Lake/Truckee is a real alternative if Sugar Bowl is the ski venue (it's the mountain Stephen's most comfortable teaching on), but it sits roughly 45 minutes further from South Lake's gondola and sno-park, so a Donner base means more driving if the group splits between mountain and lake activities on a given day.

Alameda / San Francisco

A rented apartment or house nearby

A 2–3BR short-term rental in Alameda or just across the estuary in San Francisco — close enough for easy back-and-forth to our place for meals and downtime.

~$250–450/night
South Lake Tahoe

A large vacation rental

4BR, hot tub, full kitchen, ground-floor rooms — no elevators to manage with a stroller or a cane. Usually the best fit and best value for a group this size and age range.

~$600–1,200/night for the whole group
South Lake Tahoe

The Landing Resort & Spa (alternative)

Lakefront, full-service, spa on site — a good fallback if a large enough rental isn't available for your exact dates.

~$400–700/night + resort fee
Donner Lake / Truckee (alternative)

A rental near Donner Lake

Puts you minutes from Sugar Bowl, Donner Memorial, and historic downtown Truckee. The tradeoff is the drive back to South Lake Tahoe for the gondola and the sno-park.

Closer to Sugar Bowl · farther from South Lake

DayFocusDetails
1–3Alameda & SFAlameda's Christmas Tree Lane (walkable, stroller-friendly). Ferry to San Francisco: the cable cars (the last manually operated system in the world), Mission Dolores (San Francisco's oldest building, 1776), the Ferry Building Marketplace on the way back to the dock. Presidio Tunnel Tops for an easy stroller-friendly bay view.
DayFocusDetails

Stephen takes over coaching by the afternoon.Grandparents and the baby: the Heavenly Gondola, 12 minutes up, then lunch at the mid-station deck with a lake view (a South Lake base makes this an easy add-on; from Donner it's more of a dedicated trip).

Meals & the allergy

Low shellfish risk throughout — American, Italian, and steakhouse menus dominate both the Bay Area stretch and Tahoe. Still state the allergy at booking and again with the server, every time, as standard practice.

Route 04

New Orleans

More Spanish and French colonial architecture per block than almost anywhere in the US, plus a genuinely deep musical and Creole history. Since Mom is comfortable managing her own meals here, the food culture is no longer the deciding factor — just something to plan around for everyone else.

Route7–8 nights, French Quarter-adjacent
LodgingRented house, whole group together
CharacterArchitecture, jazz, Creole history
Allergy riskHigh — Mom self-manages

Where to stay

Marigny / French Quarter-adjacent

A rented historic townhouse

Multi-bedroom Creole townhouses and shotgun houses with private courtyards are a normal rental category here — room for the whole group under one roof, with a kitchen for Mom.

~$500–900/night for the whole group
French Quarter

Hotel Monteleone (worth a visit either way)

A French Quarter landmark since 1886 — its Carousel Bar literally rotates, and its guest register reads like a syllabus (Faulkner, Tennessee Williams, and Truman Capote all stayed and wrote there). Even staying at the rental, it's worth stopping in for a drink.

Upscale · central

Day by day

DayFocusDetails
1–2Arrive & the QuarterSettle in, walk the French Quarter — Jackson Square, St. Louis Cathedral (the oldest continuously active Catholic cathedral in the US), the ironwork balconies of Royal Street.
3WWII MuseumEasily a full day for the tweens and adults; go light with the baby, or split the group.
4Streetcar & Garden DistrictThe St. Charles streetcar — the oldest continuously operating streetcar line in the world, running since 1835 — out to the Garden District for a walk among the historic mansions.
5Mardi Gras WorldA working float-building warehouse — very visual, very hands-on, a good one for the tweens.
6Whitney PlantationThe only Louisiana plantation museum told entirely from the perspective of the enslaved people who lived there — a heavier, important stop, best for tweens and adults.Grandparents and the baby take a slower morning in the Garden District instead.
7Slow morning, Quarter architectureBeignets at Café du Monde, then an unhurried, no-agenda walk through the Quarter and Faubourg Marigny's ironwork and shotgun houses.A jazz club on Frenchmen Street in the evening for whoever wants a late night.
8Honey Island swamp tourCajun Encounters' private tour of the Honey Island Swamp — a small boat (10–14 passengers) with a dedicated guide rather than the standard 22-passenger public tour. ~4.5/5 rated, gators and birdlife close to guaranteed. Roughly a half-day with pickup.
9Depart—

Meals & the allergy

This is the one stop on the list where shellfish is genuinely structural to the cuisine — gumbo and étouffée are frequently built on shrimp or crab stock even in "meat" versions, and kitchens commonly share fryers and pans across shellfish and non-shellfish dishes. Workable, since Mom plans to manage her own meals here — but worth flagging for the rest of the group too: verify at every restaurant, every time, rather than assuming a safe-sounding dish is separate from the seafood in the same kitchen.

Route 05

Southern Spain: Sevilla, Córdoba & Granada

Córdoba was, for a couple of centuries, the largest and most sophisticated city in Western Europe — paved and lit streets, public baths, and one of the great libraries of the medieval world, at a time when most of the continent had none of that. The Mezquita's forest of striped double arches wasn't decoration for its own sake: the emir who built it was a homesick exile from Damascus, and the design deliberately echoes the mosque he'd left behind. The Alhambra's palace walls are covered in the same phrase, carved thousands of times over — "there is no victor but God" — the motto of the dynasty that built it, right up until the year they lost the city. None of this is behind a single pane of glass; you walk through all of it.

Route4 nights Sevilla → 1 Córdoba → 3 Granada
LinkAVE train, Sevilla–Córdoba 45min
Book nowAlhambra tickets — sell out months out
Allergy riskModerate

Where to stay

Rentals work well in Sevilla and Granada. Córdoba's a single night, so a hotel by the Mezquita is simpler than hunting for a one-night rental.

Sevilla · Santa Cruz or Triana

A rented courtyard house

Traditional casas-patio with a plant-filled central courtyard are a normal rental category in both quarters — multiple bedrooms, a kitchen, and (in Triana especially) a few minutes' walk from the river and out of the densest tourist crowds.

~$350–600/night for the whole group
Córdoba · Judería

A hotel near the Mezquita

One night doesn't justify hunting for a rental — a mid-range hotel a few minutes' walk from the Mezquita-Catedral keeps the single evening simple.

Central · book with connecting rooms
Granada · Realejo, not Albaicín

A rented apartment on flatter ground

The Albaicín is beautiful but genuinely steep, cobbled, and hard on strollers and a cane — Realejo or around Plaza Nueva gets you nearly as close to the Alhambra without the climb. Save the Albaicín itself for the one deliberate evening walk up to the Mirador.

~$250–450/night for the whole group

Day by day

DayFocusDetails
1Arrive & SevillaLand Madrid, AVE train to Sevilla (~2.5h). Settle in, easy evening walk around Santa Cruz.
2Real Alcázar & CathedralThe Real Alcázar — a Mudéjar palace still used by the Spanish royal family today, making it the oldest palace in Europe still in active royal use. Sevilla Cathedral and the Giralda tower: the climb to the top is a ramp, not stairs, built so the muezzin could ride a horse up — easy for grandparents and a stroller alike.
3Plaza de España & TrianaPlaza de España and a slow walk through Parque de María Luisa (rowboats on the canal if anyone wants). Cross the river to Triana for its ceramics workshops. Evening: a flamenco show — Triana is the neighborhood the art form actually comes from.
4Free day, SevillaA buffer day — slower pace, a market visit, or simply repeat whatever the group liked most so far.
5CórdobaTrain to Córdoba (45 min). The Mezquita-Catedral — a mosque the size of a small city block with a Renaissance cathedral built directly inside it centuries later. The Judería (Jewish quarter) and the Roman Bridge in the evening light.
DayFocusDetails
6Transfer to GranadaA slower Córdoba morning — the Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos and its gardens — then transfer to Granada (~2h by car or bus). Evening: the walk up through the Albaicín to Mirador San Nicolás for sunset over the Alhambra.
7The AlhambraThe Nasrid Palaces and the Generalife gardens — book the timed entry months ahead, it's the single hardest reservation on this whole itinerary. Plan a slow pace; the ground is historic and uneven in places, but benches and shaded courtyards are frequent. The Generalife's gardens are flatter and an easy stretch for the baby and grandparents if the palaces themselves run long.
8Albaicín & SacromonteA daytime, unhurried walk through the Albaicín's old Moorish quarter.Evening: a flamenco show in one of the Sacromonte cave venues, for whoever wants a later night.
9DepartTrain or short flight back to Madrid, depart.

Meals & the allergy

Andalusian tapas culture has a deep bench of naturally shellfish-free staples — jamón ibérico, tortilla española, patatas bravas, salmorejo, croquetas — so a safe meal is rarely hard to find. The catch is that gambas (shrimp) and puntillitas (baby squid) are standard items on nearly every tapas menu, including ones built around ham and cheese, so it's a "check every plate" cuisine rather than a "avoid one category of restaurant" one like New Orleans.
